quotes.name: Akua Adeyemi
quotes.quote: I go into a lot of homes, and you can tell pretty quick when someone's down. It's not the mess or the dishes — it's the quiet. The TV off in the middle of the day. A chair pulled up by the window where somebody's been sitting a long time. Sometimes the medicine gets moved to the kitchen counter so it's right there where someone'll remember it. And you learn to work quiet, not to bang pipes, because somebody's sleeping in the next room. I see more of that in Chinatown than anywhere else I work. People here take care of their own — you'll see a neighbor bring soup, or a cousin come by after their shift. It's not always the hospital that carries the load. It's the family that rearranges the whole house around one sick person.

quotes.name: Deacon Seymour
quotes.quote: I spent my own stretch in a hospital bed not long ago, and I know what it's like to have your name on the door, to have people checking on you. But I also know that bed I was in—that was one bed, and there are a lot more filled by folks nobody's naming. Chinatown's carrying more sickness than anywhere else in this city, and if the ledger doesn't show them, that doesn't mean they're not there. It means nobody's counting. And when nobody's counting, people get missed. That's the part that keeps me up at night.

interviews.raw: {"answer":"quote","quote":"You want to know what a block does? We don't wait for a ledger to tell us who's sick. We know. The herbal shop lady knows who stopped coming in for their tea. The bakery knows whose order went unpicked. The seniors lunch program flyer on the board — that's not decoration, that's a lifeline. When someone's down, the shift gets covered because the person next door just shows up. Food gets brought because that's how we've always done it. And the elderly? We check. Not because a system told us to, but because Mrs. Chen's light being on at 6 a.m. is how we know she's okay. The hospital ledger can say whatever it wants. The block keeps its own books, and those books are full of names nobody's tracking.","fact_ids":["F-eb5983bccc1f","F-864011eb5188"],"basis":"lived-context","unverifiedLead":"The seniors lunch program flyer on the community bulletin board — I could ask around about who coordinates it and whether they've seen attendance drop this cycle.","abstain_reason":null}

interviews.raw: {"answer":"I've been on the other side of that ledger — lying in a hospital bed myself after my accident. And I'll tell you, when you're the one in the bed, you don't think about what neighborhood you're from. You think about getting home to your family. But those numbers — 135 sick in Chinatown — that's not a statistic to me. That's somebody's grandmother, somebody's father, somebody's kid who can't get to school. And when I look at the care trail and see nobody from that neighborhood on it, I know what that means. It means people are staying home because they can't afford not to, or they're afraid of what the bill will do to them. I've seen that fear in my own work — the paperwork, the claims, the fine print. When you're the one in the bed, you don't care about any of that. You just want someone to see you. And right now, it sounds like Chinatown isn't being seen.","fact_ids":["F-eb5983bccc1f","F-fd3a5ebe69ce"],"basis":"lived-context","unverifiedLead":null,"abstain_reason":null}
